<div class="section-heading">
# October Analyst X Data Science Huddle
</div>
**Tuesday 27th October 2026, 13:30 - 14:15, Online**

The Data Science Community for Health and Care have organised the next Analyst X Data Science Huddle for October. We will hear from one project followed by 2 practical examples of how it has been used in the NHS; see the abstract below.

* **Process Mining in the NHS**

A high-level introduction to process mining: what it is, how it works, and how it can be used to understand the way NHS services operate.

This will be followed by 2 practical examples of how it has been used in the NHS.

1. Outpatient Pathway Protocols

This example will demonstrate how process mining is applied to outpatient pathway protocols. By comparing the intended pathway with observed activity, we can identify where follow-up appointments are concentrated, understand how patients move through different pathway variants, and highlight opportunities for providers to focus improvement efforts.

The aim is not to prescribe a single solution, or a single analytical method, but to provide providers with clearer evidence about where opportunities may exist to reduce avoidable follow-ups, improve pathway efficiency, and release capacity as part of their outpatient planning.

2. Understanding Emergency Respiratory Patient Flow - Applying process mining and collaborative analytics to uncover patient flow patterns and identify improvement opportunities

This is presented as an example at Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) of executing a 'project focused' deep dive to gain insights from our rich set of disparate data.

Buit upon a robust, version-controlled data pipeline, the analysis mapped patient journeys across the respiratory pathway. This included mappings of patient movements, pathway timings, length of stay, occupancy, and daily activity patterns to provide a detailed evidence base for understanding service performance and flow.

A key principle of the project has been close collaboration with clinicians and operational teams. Recognising that data alone does not provide sufficient understanding of clinical pathways, the analysis was delivered through a series of iterative sprints. Regular review sessions enabled findings to be discussed, assumptions challenged, and priorities refined. This approach developed a shared understanding of both the service and the data, while allowing the analytical focus to adapt as new insights emerged.

This helped identify opportunities for service improvement, challenge anecdotal perceptions, as well as providing a foundation that could be built upon for future projects and more advanced predictive modelling.

<div class="section-heading">
# November Analyst X Data Science Huddle
</div>
**Tuesday 10th November 2026, 13:30 - 14:30, Online**

The Data Science Community for Health and Care have organised the next Analyst X Data Science Huddle for November. We will hear from two projects:

**Using classification and regression trees (CART) to investigate unknown ethnicity records in NHS emergency care data Presented by Grace Dean**

Time: 13:30 – 14:00

High-quality ethnicity data is necessary for tackling health inequalities. This study analysed 24.2 million Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) records from 2023/24 to (a) investigate
 variation in unknown ethnicity records, (b) explore patterns of missingness between ethnicity and other variables, and (c) identify the variables most important in the recording of an unknown ethnicity.

Variation in unknown ethnicity recording was identified by age, organisation type, and attendance characteristics. Unknown ethnicity was associated with increased missingness
 across 62 other ECDS variables. Provider site code emerged as the strongest predictor of unknown ethnicity recording, with a small number of acute trusts and independent sector organisations contributing disproportionately.

Recommendations for future work focus on improving data collection processes for individual organisations, which would provide direct benefits for NHS England and NHS providers,
 and is necessary for tackling health inequalities.

Here's a link to the paper in [BMJ Open](https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/16/8/e118200){target="_blank"}, and on the [NHS England Data Science page](https://nhsengland.github.io/datascience/mres/ethnicity/){target="_blank"}.

**Can Routine Pathway Data Identify ED Attendance Risk While Patients Wait? Presented by Kayleigh Banyard-Haydock**

Time: 14:00 – 14:30

The project investigates whether routinely collected healthcare data can be used to identify RTT elective waiting-list pathways at increased risk of emergency department attendance while awaiting treatment. It focuses on the development and evaluation of a
 prediction model that produces an individualised probability risk score using information available at the beginning of the waiting-list pathway. The model aims to support risk stratification and help identify patients who may benefit from earlier review or
 additional support, while providing a foundation for further model development. The work also considers how predicted risk could support service planning and prioritisation across these pathways.

<div class="section-heading">
# Fancy an interesting read?
</div>
Take a look at the [Why mental metaphors do not help us understand chatbot mistakes]https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11229-026-05551-8){target="_blank"} article from Springer.

Factual mistakes made by ChatGPT are frequently communicated using metaphors describing mistakes made by human minds, for example, hallucination. The article discusses this notion and demonstrates that the two most common metaphors dont't manage to provide us with a better understanding of factual chatbot mistakes. They argue that ChatGPT – and other chatbots such as Google’s Gemini by extension – do not hallucinate when they generate factually incorrect outputs, not even in a metaphorical sense. The article draws on research on hallucination in philosophy and the empirical mind sciences.

<div class="section-heading">
# Datacise Open Learning Courses
</div>

[Datacise Open Learning](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/){target="_blank"} provide training for data science in research. There are a variety of courses coming up! For more information, including how to register, follow the course link.

### [Data quality aspects of administrative data (London)](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/courses/data-quality-aspects-of-administrative-data-london/){target="_blank"}
** 6th October 2026, 09:00 - 17:00, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), London, SW1W 9SP**

This course will provide an introduction to data quality, and how it can affect all aspects of working with administrative data. The course will cover data quality dimensions which include technical and social aspects.

### [Introduction to Government, Policy & Impact](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/courses/introduction-to-government-policy-impact/){target="_blank"}
**11th November 2026, 09:30 - 15:15, Live Online**

This course explores different experiences of successfully engaging with policy makers, so that research evidence has a greater impact and influence. The course aims to be engaging, informative, interactive, and practical, with opportunities to share experiences from your research.

### [Good Practice for R Users When Working in the ONS SRS](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/courses/good-practice-for-r-users-when-working-in-the-ons-srs/){target="_blank"}
**25th November 2026, 14:00 - 15:00, Online**

A practical workshop on writing efficient, reproducible and robust R code when working with large administrative datasets in the ONS Secure Research Service. Drawing on real-world SRS experience, the session will cover analytical workflow design, efficient database queries, memory management, safe joins, validation and reproducibility.

### [Ethical AI Coding with Synthetic Administrative Data](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/courses/ethical-ai-coding-with-synthetic-administrative-data/){target="_blank"}
**20th November 2026, 09:30 - 16:00, UK Research & Innovation, London SW1W 9SP and Online**

This course explores the ethical use of local AI models for developing code to analyse synthetic administrative data, combining practical skills training with examples of best practice.

### [ADR UK Determining Healthy Households](https://dataciseopenlearning.org/courses/adr-uk-determining-healthy-households/){target="_blank"}
**Self-paced, Online**

A self-paced course on how to create Household Units of Analysis (HUAs) from line-level pseudonymised GP patient data.

### [AI in the NHS 2026](https://www.health.org.uk/events/ai-in-the-nhs-2026){target="_blank"}
**Thursday 15 October 2026, 10.00–17.00, Online**

2026 is set to be a pivotal year for AI in the NHS, with important national strategies and regulatory reforms expected that will impact what kinds of technologies get used and how the health service adopts and oversees them.

But turning the vision of an AI-enabled health system into reality won’t be straightforward. Our third annual AI event will bring together stakeholders from across the NHS, government, industry, academia and the charity sector to consider how the NHS can responsibly, safely and effectively implement AI at scale.

This full day event will explore how to:

* translate national strategy into real-world implementation
* evaluate and scale AI tools rapidly, safely and effectively
* build trust among clinicians, patients and the public
* support the workforce through technological transformation
* learn from leading international health systems already using AI at scale.
